title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.0

hero.subtitle: The original request/response protocol that launched the World Wide Web

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/1.0 is the version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol that this RFC documents, reflecting common usage in 1996. It defines the basic request/response model that underlies all communication on the World Wide Web.

The World-Wide Web global information initiative has used HTTP since 1990. This RFC documents HTTP/1.0 as an informational record of common usage, and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.eli5: Long ago a few people made a way for computers to ask each other for web pages. This paper writes down how most of them already did it.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
HTTP is a stateless, request/response protocol. A client sends a request message to a server, and the server returns a response message.

Stateless
Each request is independent. The server retains no memory of previous requests from the same client. State management (sessions, cookies) must be built on top.
Text-Based
HTTP/1.0 messages are human-readable text. Request and response headers are ASCII text lines terminated by CRLF.
One Request Per Connection
In HTTP/1.0, each request opens a new TCP connection, sends the request, receives the response, and closes the connection. This is simple but inefficient.
sections.eli5: The browser asks, the server answers, and then they hang up. The server does not remember you between asks, like a clerk who forgets each customer as soon as they leave the counter.

sections.title: Request
sections.content:
An HTTP request consists of a request line, headers, and an optional body:

HTTP/1.0 Request Format
GET /index.html HTTP/1.0
User-Agent: CERN-LineMode/2.15 libwww/2.17b3
Accept: text/html
MethodThe action to perform (GET, POST, HEAD)Token
Request-URIThe resource being requestedURI
HTTP-Version"HTTP/1.0" for requests made under this specificationString
sections.eli5: A request is a short note. The first line says what you want and which thing you want it from, then come a few extra lines about you, then a blank line.

sections.title: Response
sections.content:
An HTTP response consists of a status line, headers, and an optional body:

HTTP/1.0 Response Format
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1234

<html>...</html>
sections.eli5: The answer starts with a line saying how it went, such as "OK". Then come some details about the thing, a blank line, and the thing itself.

sections.title: Methods
sections.eli5: There are three main things you can ask. "Give me that", "just tell me about that" and "here, take this and do something with it".

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers grouped by category:

200 OKThe request has succeeded
301 Moved PermanentlyResource has been permanently moved
304 Not ModifiedResource has not changed since last request
400 Bad RequestServer cannot process the request due to client error
404 Not FoundThe requested resource could not be found
500 Internal Server ErrorUnexpected server-side error
sections.eli5: The first number of the answer tells you how it went. 2 means good, 3 means go look somewhere else, 4 means you asked wrong, and 5 means the server broke.

references.text: Fielding, R., et al., "Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.1", RFC 2616, June 1999.
Berners-Lee, T., "Universal Resource Identifiers in WWW: A Unifying Syntax for the Expression of Names and Addresses of Objects on the Network as used in the World-Wide Web", RFC 1630, June 1994.

subtitle: The request/response protocol that launched the World Wide Web.

eli5.summary: Your browser asks a web computer for a page by sending one short text note, and the web computer sends back a note with the page inside.

tldr.problem: The Web had been using HTTP since 1990, but practice varied and nothing recorded what most clients and servers actually did.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a connection, sends a request line (method, URI, version), optional headers, a blank line and maybe a body. The server replies with a status line, headers, a blank line and the entity, then closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: It documented common practice, with GET, HEAD and POST, and was followed by HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068, then RFC 2616). The IESG noted that it expected a standards-track replacement soon.

questions: what is the difference between http 1.0 and http 1.1
what does a 404 status code mean
how does an http request look
why does http 1.0 close the connection after each request
today: HTTP/1.0 is still understood by almost every web server and proxy, and the basic shape it documented (request line, headers, blank line, body) carries through HTTP/1.1. The semantics now live in RFC 9110 and the text format in RFC 9112, while HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same messages in binary form. You can still see HTTP/1.0 behavior in simple tools and legacy clients that open one connection per request.

facts.label: Connection
facts.value: Opened per request, closed by the server

viz.caption: one request, one response, one connection

messages.label: GET /index.html HTTP/1.0 + headers + blank line
messages.note: The client establishes the connection before each request, normally TCP port 80.

messages.label: HTTP/1.0 200 OK + headers + blank line + entity body
messages.note: The server sends a Status-Line, response and entity headers, then the entity body.

messages.label: Server closes the connection
messages.note: Current practice is that the connection is closed by the server after sending the response.

items.label: Retrieve
items.desc: Retrieve whatever information is identified by the Request-URI. Becomes a conditional GET when If-Modified-Since is present.

items.label: Headers only
items.desc: Identical to GET except that the server must not return any Entity-Body.

items.label: Submit
items.desc: Ask the server to accept the enclosed entity as a new subordinate of the Request-URI. A valid Content-Length is required.

items.label: Informational
items.desc: Not used, but reserved for future use.

items.label: Success
items.desc: The action was successfully received, understood, and accepted.

items.label: Redirection
items.desc: Further action must be taken in order to complete the request.

items.label: Client Error
items.desc: The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled.

items.label: Server Error
items.desc: The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.
